summary: Describes an RTP payload format for carrying the coordinates of a dynamic pointer, such as a laser pointer, used during a presentation. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a speaker points at a slide, this sends where the pointer is, so viewers far away see the dot move as well.

questions: what is the rtp pointer payload format
how are pointer coordinates encoded in rtp
what is the pointer icon number in rtp
subtitle: An RTP payload format that sends a presenter's pointer position separately from the slides, in four bytes.

tldr.problem: In remote presentations the pointer needs high temporal resolution to stay in sync with the speaker's words, while the slides need high spatial resolution, and video good enough for both is expensive or needs huge bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The pointer coordinates are captured and sent on their own as RTP packets, each carrying a 12-bit x and y position, three effect flags and a 3-bit icon number, timestamped with a 90kHz clock.
tldr.outcome: A simple, cheap pointer stream that viewers can display in step with audio and video, registered as the MIME type video/pointer. It is deliberately not a general mouse event protocol.

facts.label: Coordinate size
facts.value: 12 bits each for x and y

today: RFC 2862 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Send the Pointer Separately
sections.content:
RFC 2862 defines an RTP payload format for the coordinates of a dynamic pointer used during a presentation. Presentations convey much of their information through viewgraphs and a pointer, so both must be transmitted accurately in remote conferencing.

The problem with plain video of the presenter's display is that viewgraphs need high spatial resolution, while pointer movements must be sampled at high temporal resolution so the pointing shows up in sync with the audio and video. The RFC's example is a speaker pointing at two alternatives in turn while saying "this one is better than this". Doing both with one video stream may need at least S-VHS quality video, and the codecs for that are expensive, while uncompressed video needs very high bandwidth.

The proposed alternative is a simpler and cheaper system that captures and transmits the pointer coordinates separately. The document also says that a mouse can be the pointer, but the format is not intended for, and may lack the functions needed by, a general mouse event transmission mechanism.
sections.eli5: Sending a whole movie just to show a moving dot is wasteful. It is cheaper to send only where the dot is, many times a second.

sections.title: How the Coordinates Are Captured
sections.content:
The RFC describes several ways to get pointer coordinates relative to a displayed viewgraph. In electronic presentation systems they are easy to obtain. For optical systems such as overhead transparencies, the viewgraph can be captured into a frame buffer on a computer. A document camera and a video capture card can capture transparencies, printed material or even three dimensional objects, and electronic viewgraphs can be fed in through the capture card too.

A side benefit is that a presenter's own computer can transmit electronic viewgraphs without connecting to, for example, an intranet. The captured image is shown with the capturing computer's mouse pointer on the presenter's display through a projector. The presenter moves the pointer with a regular or wireless mouse, and software on the capturing computer captures its location.
sections.eli5: A computer watches the slide and also notices where the presenter's mouse dot is. It sends the dot's position to everyone else.

sections.title: The Payload Format
sections.content:
An RTP packet for this format has the normal RTP header followed directly by the pointer data. The format has no payload specific header.

The payload packs the following into 32 bits: three flag bits L, M and R, a 12-bit x-coordinate, a 3-bit PIN (Pointer Icon Number), and a 12-bit y-coordinate, with the unused bits marked as must-be-zero in the figure.

The x and y values are measured from the upper left corner of the associated display window. Each is a fraction of the corresponding edge length of the window, held as a 12-bit, positive, fixed point number between 0 and (1 - 2^-12).

The L (left), R (right) and M (middle) bits are pointer special effects flags. Their use is application dependent and MUST be established out-of-band, and applications MAY ignore them. The PIN selects a pointer icon; the mapping from numbers to pictures MUST also be set up out-of-band. PIN 0 is the default icon, applications with one icon SHOULD set it to zero, and receivers MAY ignore non-zero values and show a default icon.
sections.eli5: Each message is like a tiny note saying how far across and how far down the dot is, which button effects are on, and which dot picture to use.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
Most RTP header fields follow the base RTP specification (RFC 1889): the sequence number, SSRC, CC and CSRC fields are used as described there, and RTCP SHOULD be used as defined there.

The format-specific rules are few. The timestamp is the sampling time of the pointer location, measured by a 90kHz clock. The marker (M) bit is set to one if the pointer icon changes in this packet. The extension (X) bit is defined by the RTP profile in use.

The payload type is not assigned here. The RFC expects the RTP profile for a class of applications to assign one, or else a payload type in the dynamic range to be chosen.
sections.eli5: The envelope follows the usual RTP rules. The time stamp says when the dot was at that spot, and a special flag shouts when the dot picture changes.

sections.title: MIME Registration
sections.content: The document defines a new RTP payload name, pointer, and the associated MIME subtype video/pointer. The registration lists no required or optional parameters and no magic numbers or file extensions. It names videoconferencing systems that transmit viewgraphs with a real-time pointer as the applications that use the type, and gives its intended usage as COMMON.
sections.eli5: The format gets an official name tag, video/pointer, so programs can recognize it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Packets in this format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification. The RFC adds that the payload type does not show any significant non-uniformity in receiver computational complexity for packet processing, so it does not create a potential denial-of-service threat from that source.
sections.eli5: Handling these small messages is always about equally easy, so nobody can easily overload a receiver with them. Other safety rules come from RTP itself.

fields.name: x-coordinate
fields.desc: Fraction of window width from the left edge.

fields.name: PIN
fields.desc: Pointer Icon Number; 0 is the default icon.

fields.name: y-coordinate
fields.desc: Fraction of window height from the top edge.
